# My grooming van almost caught fire. Here’s what I’ve learned since.

Last Wednesday, October 28, around 2:15 p.m., I was parked in a client’s driveway in Bedford, drying Moose on high.

Moose is a Bernese mountain dog, which means drying him is less “using a hair dryer” and more “trying to remove weather from a large, friendly carpet.” I had done everything the way I normally do. He was clean, the van was running, and I was thinking about how much coat was still hiding underneath the coat I could see.

Then I smelled hot plastic.

My first thought was the dryer motor. I actually remember being annoyed, because of course the dryer would die in the middle of Moose. Then I saw smoke coming from the bench seat where my batteries are.

I shut off the battery switch, got Moose out through the side door, and used the extinguisher briefly. I honestly don’t know whether I needed to or whether switching everything off had already stopped what was happening. There were no dramatic flames. When I looked at the cable afterwards, the lug was black and the insulation had melted back by roughly three centimetres.

Moose was still damp and absolutely delighted by this change in the schedule. Everyone was okay. That is the most important sentence in this whole post.

I’m writing the rest of it because my van almost caught fire because of things I didn’t know to check, and because Tasha is about to pay a deposit to the same person who built mine. I also know other mobile groomers read this. A lot of us are running serious electrical equipment in small vans and trusting that the tidy-looking installation behind the cupboard door was done properly.

Mine looked tidy.

Tidy is not the same as right.

Before I get into the numbers: **I am not an electrician.** I am a dog groomer with a notebook, an insurance claim that may or may not go anywhere, and three weeks minimum without my workplace. The electrical findings below come from Priya at Sackville Marine Electric, who came out after the incident and explained what she found. Her cable-size recommendation and repair plan are for my particular setup. Please don’t copy them into a cart and call your own van inspected.

## What my setup was

Coastline Van Fitouts — Darren — built the van in spring 2025.

The relevant equipment was:

- A 3,000 W inverter
- Two 200 Ah lithium batteries
- A 12 V battery system
- A 4 AWG cable run between the battery bank and inverter
- A 300 A ANL fuse
- My high-velocity dryer, which draws roughly 1,800–2,000 W in use
- A water heater that sometimes cycles on as well

I bought a professionally built van because I did not want to become an expert in any of this. I wanted clean dogs, warm water, and a workplace that didn’t scare me. When I opened the bench, everything looked secured and covered and intentional. There was heat-shrink on the connections. The cupboards were neat. I took that as evidence that somebody had done the underlying calculations.

That was my mistake.

## Priya’s first concern: the cable was far too small for this installation

Priya told me that, for my 3,000 W inverter on a 12 V system, the main battery-to-inverter cable should have been 2/0, based on my installation and expected use. What was installed was 4 AWG.

Those labels meant nothing to me before last week, so here is the basic version without me pretending I can now design your van.

Watts, volts and amps are related by a simple bit of math:

**amps = watts ÷ volts**

That’s the tidy starting point, not the whole design calculation.

At 12 V:

- 1,800 W ÷ 12 V = 150 A
- 2,000 W ÷ 12 V = about 167 A
- 3,000 W ÷ 12 V = 250 A

So when my dryer is drawing 1,800–2,000 W, the simple calculation already puts the load around 150–167 A at 12 V. With the water heater sometimes running as well, the demand can climb beyond that. The notes I made after Priya left put the plausible operating range at roughly 150–250 A or more, depending on what was running.

And the real battery current is higher than that simple division suggests. The inverter is not perfectly efficient. It wastes some power as heat. Battery voltage also does not sit at exactly 12 V under load; as voltage drops, the current needed for the same power goes up. A dryer and water heater can also behave differently when starting or cycling.

I don’t have a log telling me the exact current at 2:15 p.m., so I’m not going to invent one. The point is that this wasn’t a little occasional load. Drying a big dog on high can ask a 12 V system for a very large, sustained current.

There also isn’t one universal internet chart that says, “every 3,000 W inverter must always use this exact cable.” Cable length matters. Voltage drop matters. The insulation’s temperature rating, how the cable is routed, whether it’s bundled, the surrounding temperature, the connections and the inverter manufacturer’s instructions all matter too.

But that is exactly why the person building the van needs to show their work.

For scale, 4 AWG copper has a conductor cross-section of about 21 mm². A 2/0 conductor is about 67 mm². The 2/0 cable Priya specified isn’t a slightly skinnier-looking upgrade. It has roughly three times the conductor cross-section.

My system wasn’t protecting some small inverter that I occasionally used to charge a laptop. It was supporting my income, my water heating and a dryer running hard beside a wet Bernese.

## The second problem was hidden under heat-shrink

The lug on the positive end had not been crimped with a proper crimper.

Under the heat-shrink, Priya showed me evidence that it had been crushed with something like pliers or a hammer. From the outside, it looked finished. The heat-shrink covered the part that would have told a different story.

A proper crimp is not just “metal squeezed onto wire until it stays.” The lug and cable need to match, and the crimp needs to be made with the right tool and method so the conductor and connector form a secure, low-resistance connection. The lug also needs proper support and strain relief. Heat-shrink can help seal and protect a connection. It does not turn a bad crimp into a good one.

Priya explained why a poor connection matters so much at these currents. Heat at a connection isn’t just about whether something feels loosely attached. Electrical resistance creates heat, and the heating rises with the **square** of the current.

Her simplified example was this: at 200 A, even a resistance of just 0.001 ohm at a bad connection would produce 40 W of heat right there.

That wasn’t a measurement of my lug. It was an illustration of why a tiny defect can become a serious local hot spot when you’re running grooming equipment. Forty watts concentrated in the wrong little area, surrounded by cable insulation and enclosed cabinetry, is not something I want beside my dogs.

If you doubled the current in that example, you wouldn’t merely double the heating at that same resistance. You would quadruple it.

I cannot tell you which single defect “started it.” I don’t think anyone can rewind Wednesday and prove the precise first link in the chain from a photograph. What Priya found was a combination:

- Very high sustained current
- A main cable she considered substantially undersized for the installation
- A badly made positive connection hidden by heat-shrink
- Fuse placement that left much more battery cable before the fuse than she wanted to see

The black lug and the insulation melted back around three centimetres are consistent with me being extremely lucky that I smelled it when I did.

## The fuse was not where Priya said it should be

My main fuse was a 300 A ANL fuse, mounted approximately 90 cm from the battery.

Priya told me it should have been within roughly 18 cm — about seven inches — in the kind of installation she was assessing. There can be design details and applicable standards that affect the exact requirement, so again, ask a qualified person about your own van rather than treating a sentence on my blog as the electrical code.

The principle made immediate sense once she explained it.

The fuse is supposed to protect the circuit, including the wiring. If there is a long cable run between the battery and the fuse, that section does not have the nearby overcurrent protection you might assume it has. Ninety centimetres is roughly five times the distance Priya was talking about.

The rating matters too. A 300 A fuse does not magically make a 4 AWG main cable suitable for a 3,000 W, 12 V inverter. The fuse and cable need to be selected together. Among other things, you want the protection to operate before the smallest conductor it is meant to protect becomes the problem.

A fuse also cannot be relied upon to catch every bad crimp. A high-resistance connection can get dangerously hot while the circuit is still drawing less than the fuse’s rating. The fuse can sit there doing its job perfectly while heat builds at a connection elsewhere.

Priya’s repair quote includes replacing the main runs, installing a new fuse block and using a Class T fuse. She explained that Class T fuses have a high interrupt capacity and are commonly used for main battery protection in lithium systems. In plain language, the device has to be able to safely interrupt the sort of fault current the battery bank can deliver, not just carry the normal operating current.

That does **not** mean every ANL fuse is automatically unsafe or that everyone should order a Class T fuse tonight. The replacement has to suit the battery bank, system voltage, conductors and equipment. What I’m taking from it is that “there is a fuse” is not enough information. Ask what type it is, what it’s rated for, where it is, and why it was chosen.

And never put in a bigger fuse because the old one keeps blowing. That is disabling a warning, not fixing a circuit.

## The thermal camera comparison was the part that really got me

Priya showed me my damage photos alongside thermal camera images from her own van running a similar kind of load.

Her connections and cables barely got warm.

That wasn’t a controlled scientific comparison of my van before the incident. But seeing the two things next to each other made the problem feel very real. I had assumed warmth was just what happened when equipment worked hard. I didn’t know what normal looked like, so I had no baseline for abnormal.

Since then, I bought an infrared thermometer for about $40 at Canadian Tire. I think every mobile groomer should have one.

Not because it turns you into an electrician. It doesn’t. A $40 thermometer cannot certify your wiring, reveal every bad connection, or tell you that your van is safe.

What it can do is measure surface temperatures and help you notice a change or an unexpected hot spot under normal use, after a professional has confirmed that the system is safe to operate. You can build a baseline for your own setup and compare similar points under similar loads.

There are limitations. Shiny metal can give misleading infrared readings. Distance, angle and the surface material matter. An infrared reading only tells you about the surface you’re measuring. If nothing is running, a connection may show nothing unusual. A normal-looking reading is not permission to ignore a smell, discolouration, smoke or damaged insulation.

Still, for $40, it is a lot better than waiting until your client’s dog is half dry and your bench is smoking.

## My smoke alarm situation was not good either

There was no smoke detector in the back of my van.

The only one was in the cab, and that came with the van. I was relying on my own nose while working a few feet away from a noisy dryer.

A working alarm in the grooming area could provide earlier warning. It would not have corrected the cable, repaired the crimp or moved the fuse. It is another layer, not a repair.

I’m asking Priya about appropriate detection for the rear workspace, including placement and a unit suitable for the conditions in a van. Whatever is installed needs to be tested and maintained. I’m also reviewing my extinguisher, its rating and where it’s mounted rather than just being vaguely pleased that I own one.

If you see smoke, don’t stand there trying to diagnose which appliance is responsible. Stop using the system if it is safe to do so, get yourself and any animals out, move away and call emergency services. Lithium battery incidents and electrical fires are not the moment for a Groomer Facebook Group poll.

For the record, Priya’s findings were about the cable and connection. I am not claiming my battery cells caught fire. They didn’t.

## A checklist you can actually do on your own van

This is a **visual and paperwork checklist**, not an electrical inspection.

Turn off the inverter and connected loads and switch off the main battery disconnect if your system is designed for you to do that. Follow the shutdown instructions for your own equipment.

Please understand that switching off the inverter does **not** make the battery system harmless. Battery cables and terminals can remain energized even when everything appears off. Shore power, solar and other charging sources can add complications. If you are not completely sure how your system is isolated, stop at reading labels and book a professional.

Do not remove heat-shrink, open sealed electrical enclosures, loosen terminals, pull on crimps or stick tools into anything. If you find heat damage or smell burning, do not turn the system back on to see whether it happens again.

### 1. Find out what inverter you actually have

Read the nameplate and manual.

Write down:

- Continuous output in watts
- Surge or peak output, listed separately
- DC input voltage
- The manufacturer’s cable and fuse requirements

Do not confuse a big surge number with what it can supply continuously. My concern is the equipment I run for long stretches, not an impressive number on a sales listing.

### 2. Write down your realistic grooming load

Include more than the dryer.

Think about:

- The dryer on its highest normal setting
- Water heater
- Clippers, lights and fans
- Air conditioning, if you have it
- Laptop, phone and battery charging
- Anything that might cycle on while you’re drying a dog

If two heavy loads are not supposed to run together, ask how that is prevented. A verbal “just don’t use both” is not much of a system design when you’re alone, busy and running late.

Note the wattage printed on the appliances, but have a professional calculate the actual DC side. Don’t just add up all the outlets and guess.

### 3. Find the visible cable markings

Without dismantling anything, see whether you can read the gauge printed on the main positive and negative battery-to-inverter cables.

Record:

- Cable size, such as 4 AWG or 2/0
- Approximate length and route
- Any visible insulation or temperature-rating information
- Whether the positive and negative main runs appear to be the same size

If you see 4 AWG on a system like mine, treat that as a reason for an urgent professional review, not as a DIY diagnosis from my blog.

### 4. Locate the main fuse and measure roughly how far it is from the battery

Read the label on the fuse and holder.

Write down:

- Amperage
- Fuse type, such as ANL or Class T
- Approximate distance from the battery
- Whether the holder and surrounding material show heat damage

Ask the electrician whether its rating, location and interrupt capacity protect the actual cable and suit your particular battery bank.

### 5. Look for changes, not just obvious disasters

Pay attention to:

- Brown, yellow or black discolouration
- Melted or shrivelled insulation
- Cracked insulation
- A hot plastic or fishy electrical smell
- Corrosion
- Cable rubbing against metal or a sharp edge
- Missing supports or strain relief
- Connections exposed to water, dog hair or grooming chemicals
- Anything that looks different from your build photos

A cable can look neat while still being undersized. A crimp can look neat because somebody covered it. That’s why the next step matters.

### 6. Ask how the connections were made

“Was a proper crimper used?” is a start, but ask for specifics:

- What lug was used?
- Was it matched to the cable?
- What crimping tool and die were used?
- Is there a photo from before it was covered with heat-shrink?
- How is the lug supported so vibration and cable weight aren’t stressing it?

Do not tug on a battery connection to test it yourself.

### 7. Check the boring emergency details

Can you reach the battery disconnect quickly? Do you know what it shuts off and what it doesn’t?

Is your extinguisher accessible, inspected and suitable? Do you have working detection in the workspace, installed according to its instructions? Can you get a large dog out through a second door if your usual exit is blocked?

My emergency plan had mostly consisted of owning an extinguisher and hoping for the best.

### 8. Get an independent electrical inspection

Find a qualified 12 V/mobile electrical professional who has experience with high-current inverters and lithium battery systems. Tell them your actual grooming loads, not just “it’s a 3,000 W inverter.”

Ask them to assess the design, cable sizes, connections, fusing, disconnects, cable routing and battery limits. If you already own an infrared thermometer or thermal camera, ask them what would be useful to monitor after the system has been deemed safe.

A visual glance at the bench is not the same thing.

## Tasha: please get this in writing before you pay the deposit

This applies to Darren, and it applies to any builder. It applies even if the builder is lovely. It applies if their Instagram is beautiful. It especially applies if they make you feel silly for asking.

Before a deposit, ask for a written electrical design or specification that includes:

1. **The inverter’s continuous rating and DC system voltage.**

2. **The expected continuous DC current**, based on how you will actually groom, including which loads can operate together.

3. **The battery bank’s continuous discharge capability**, including the BMS limits. Two batteries being 200 Ah each does not, by itself, answer whether the whole system is correctly designed.

4. **The main positive and negative cable sizes and run lengths**, plus the reasoning for those sizes and the manufacturer requirements being followed.

5. **The voltage-drop calculation** for the main inverter run.

6. **The main fuse type, amperage, voltage rating and interrupt rating**, along with its planned location and distance from the battery.

7. **The branch circuit protection and disconnects**, not just the big main fuse.

8. **The connector and crimping method**, including the lugs and tools that will be used.

9. **Cable support, chafe protection and strain relief**, because vans vibrate and move.

10. **The standard or manufacturer instructions the installation is being designed to meet**, and who is responsible for checking it.

11. **A final load test under realistic grooming conditions**, ideally including temperature checks or thermal imaging at appropriate points.

12. **Permission for an independent qualified electrician to review the design** and inspect the finished installation.

Ask for the complete parts list too. A line in a quote that says “full electrical package” tells you almost nothing.

If the answers are vague, keep asking. If the builder says the cable is “heavy-duty,” ask for the gauge. If they say it has “plenty of fuse,” ask for the type, rating and location. If they say your dryer won’t be a problem, ask them to show you the calculation using your actual dryer and water heater.

A good professional should be able to explain their choices without making you feel stupid. Getting it in writing gives everyone something clear to build to and inspect.

And if you already own a grooming van, you do not need to wait until you’re buying another one. Make the appointment now.

## About Darren

I’m not interested in writing a dramatic takedown. I also don’t want to soften the facts until they become useless.

Darren built my van. This is what Priya found in it. As of writing this, he has not responded to three texts and an email from me since the incident.

People can draw their own conclusions from that. Mine is simply that I should have asked for the electrical specifications before I paid, rather than trusting neat cupboards and heat-shrink.

## Where things stand now

The repair quote is **$4,200**. That covers rewiring the main runs, a new fuse block and a Class T fuse, along with the associated work. Priya has said **three weeks minimum**, with parts on order.

I have cancelled **31 appointments** so far.

Insurance has said “maybe,” in that special insurance way where the word technically contains hope but does not help you pay for anything. The adjuster is coming Thursday.

My whole income is that van. Rent is due on the first, and I am scared. I keep replaying what would have happened if I had stepped outside for a minute, if Moose had been crated differently, if I had dismissed the smell as the dryer for another five minutes. I know those thoughts aren’t useful, but they’re here anyway.

Moose’s mom brought me a coffee and sat with me on her steps while I shook. I don’t think she realizes how much that helped. There was no “at least” in it, no lecture about what I should have known. She just sat there while I tried to become a functioning person again.

Moose, for his part, went home slightly damp and completely unbothered.

Please check your vans. Buy the cheap infrared thermometer, but don’t use it as a substitute for an inspection. Get the cable sizes, loads, fuse specifications and connection methods in writing. If somebody tells you not to worry because everything is “done properly,” ask them to show you what properly means.

I thought I had a safe van because it looked professional. Now I know that a finish you can see is not proof of the work you can’t.

I’ll post another update when the van is repaired and back on the road. Right now, everyone is alive, Moose is fine, and I’m very, very tired of being at home.
